html:
Small sea shells called nzimbu, or zimbos, were the money of the kingdom of Kongo. They were gathered on the island off Luanda, and the king of Kongo controlled the fishing grounds. Control of the shells was control of the money supply.

That changed when Portugal founded the town of Luanda in 1576 and built up the colony of Angola. The Portuguese took over the shell beds and later brought in shells from Brazil. More shells meant each one bought less, and the king's wealth and power shrank. Raffia cloth also served as money in the region.

Shell money was common in Africa. Cowries from the Maldives were used across West Africa, and copper manillas in the Niger delta. The Kongo case shows how a foreign power could weaken a state by flooding its currency.
